rv.q: Everything that was very right about Daniel Sullivan's staging in Central Park last summer is even more impressive indoors, especially Lily Rabe as a Portia who begins with strength and wit and grows into devastating self-knowledge.
Daniel Sullivan's absolutely splendid production of 'The Merchant of Venice' at the Broadhurst Theater

When I reviewed The Public Theater's Central Park production of "The Merchant of Venice" back in June, I said that it might well end up on Broadway, and that it deserved to. This has now happened, and the main reason for the transfer is, needless to say, the presence of Al Pacino in the cast. Even s...
This transfer is dear bought, that’s for sure.
Bringing illuminating insights to the headstrong heiress Portia, the young actress is the production’s real treasure.
She reaches into our hearts and haunts our minds, as this Merchant does in general.
Their combined work represents nothing short of a master class in acting Shakespeare.
Add dramatic lighting by Kenneth Posner and jolly wigs, dances and scuffles, and credit Sullivan’s engaging conception of the play.
No doubt a villain in Pacino's merciless portrayal, even the interpolation of a cruel baptismal sequence secures little sympathy for this dangerous character.
Sullivan’s production and Pacino’s performance are memorable events that underline the complexity and depth of Shakespeare’s understanding and critique of the times.

cn.t: Pacino's haunting Shylock and Rabe's radiant Portia anchor Sullivan's splendid, pitch-perfect production that brings gripping clarity to Shakespeare's troubling play, making it a blockbuster hit.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's least comfortable theaters, with notoriously tight legroom and narrow seats. The lack of rake means tall patrons in front block your view. Restrooms are in the basement, creating long intermission lines. For legroom, target Row A or N in Orchestra.

acc.note: 6 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
